video_title: Eric Schmidt: Are We Ready for Superintelligence? | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Eric Schmidt tells Nicolai Tangen that AI is not a bubble (Anthropic's revenue growth has beaten Google's record), that agents will flatten companies and remove 'glue' roles, and that AGI is 5-10 years away. He also says Europe is losing through over-regulation, China trails the US by about six months but wins users with free open-weight models, and AI-driven misinformation threatens democracy.

themes.theme: AI capex is real demand, not a bubble

insights.claim: Eric Schmidt argues AI is not a bubble because Anthropic's revenue growth has more than doubled the speed of Google's record-setting revenue growth from his CEO era, with real paying customers.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Counters AI-bubble narratives; supports continued spend on AI infrastructure and model-lab valuations.
insights.quote: If you look at anthropics revenue growth, when I was CEO at Google, we set the revenue growth record. They smashed it more than twice the speed as we did.

insights.claim: The AI wave is driven not only by algorithmic breakthroughs but by 'scale compute': 2-nanometer chips largely made in Taiwan, big memory improvements and data centers of almost incomprehensible power.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Keeps the compute supply chain (leading-edge foundry, memory, data center builders) at the center of the AI trade, with Taiwan concentration risk.

insights.claim: Frontier models take about six months to build and two months to test, cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and are obsolete within about five months of release, so the product cycle is shorter than the build cycle.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Fast depreciation of model investments means durable moats are hard to hold; favors players with distribution and compute scale over any single model.
insights.quote: The models, for example, take roughly six months to build, two months or so to actually test, and they're released, and they're antiquated within five months.

insights.claim: Schmidt says the competition for AI leadership is more brutal than PC vs Mac or Android vs iPhone, with the lead moving between Anthropic and OpenAI on deep reasoning while Google and Meta each claim their next model will win.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Expect price pressure and leadership churn among model labs; avoid betting on a single model leader.

insights.claim: Schmidt expects the next competitive cycle among AI labs to compress from months to days.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Signals ever-faster obsolescence and rising pressure on margins for model providers.

insights.claim: In roughly the last month, AI helped solve 10 major math problems previously thought unsolvable; Schmidt sees math as the start of every next scientific revolution, potentially feeding physics and better batteries over a decade.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Watch AI-for-science as a source of downstream breakthroughs in energy and materials.
insights.quote: Math is the beginning of every next revolution.

insights.claim: Current AI can know every fact and write all code, but genuine discovery is still out of reach: a model trained on math known in 1902 cannot yet discover general relativity.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: A useful test for separating knowledge-retrieval AI from true discovery AI when judging AGI claims.
insights.quote: I was a professional programmer. My job is dead, right?

insights.claim: Schmidt thinks the most promising path to AI discovery is cross-domain pattern transfer (applying techniques from one field to another) rather than pure reinforcement-learning randomness, and puts AGI at 5 to 10 years away.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Sets a medium-term AGI horizon; near-term value comes from automation, not discovery.
insights.quote: It's somewhere between my estimate is 5 to 10 years.

insights.claim: AI gains are fastest in 'scale-free' domains (software, cyber and math) where systems get rapid feedback or need no new data, and slowest where data collection is hard, such as biology, physics and chemistry.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Expect software and cyber disruption first; AI-bio timelines will lag due to data scarcity, making data-generation assets valuable.
insights.quote: So the industry is moving the fastest in what are called the scale-free parts and will be the slowest where the data collection is horrible.

insights.claim: Because writing code and writing cyberattacks are the same skill, AI coding gains have created a large new set of cyber threats.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Supports structural demand for cybersecurity products as offensive AI capability grows.
insights.quote: writing software is the same as writing soft cyber attacks. It's just it's just evil, right?

insights.claim: Schmidt has friends, including Demis Hassabis by implication, who believe AI could cure all human disease in the next 15 to 20 years, though biology is constrained by lack of training data.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Long-dated optionality in AI drug discovery; data bottleneck is the gating factor.

insights.claim: Many people believe superintelligence will arrive within a few years in specific categories, such as visual and robotic superintelligence, rather than as a single general system.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Look for domain-specific foundation models and startups as the investable form of superintelligence.

insights.claim: Schmidt frames agents as input, then reasoning and many activities, then a summary, and argues almost every business workflow (design, manufacturing, assembly, servicing) is a chain of concatenated agents that, combined with slower-arriving robots, could replace human workflows.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Lens for identifying which industries' workflows are most exposed to agentic automation.

insights.claim: Anthropic's Claude tools sitting in Slack let a CEO monitor everyone's work, detect data exfiltration and get instant summaries, making organizations flatter, smarter, more intense and faster.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI monitoring and coordination tools are a large market; expect leaner management layers.

insights.claim: Anthropic writes most of its own code with its own models, a huge productivity shift that other software companies will adopt only as fast as their leadership and technical strength allow.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Software firms with strong technical leadership will widen margins first; laggards face disruption.

insights.claim: Schmidt believes almost none of today's established companies will make the cultural changes AI requires; startups will pioneer and large firms follow late, with information-centric sectors like stock markets at the tip of the spear.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Favor AI-native challengers over incumbents; expect slow enterprise adoption curves outside tech and finance.
insights.quote: I have a strong view that almost none of the companies that are listening to this will actually do the necessary changes in their culture.

insights.claim: AI can eliminate much of the 'coordination tax' in large companies; Schmidt estimates a 10,000-person company has a couple of thousand people it does not need, chiefly 'glue' roles doing planning and moving numbers around.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Supports margin expansion via headcount reduction; expect layoffs concentrated in middle/coordination roles.
insights.quote: My guess is you've got a couple of thousand people who you don't need

insights.claim: A fast-growing company cited by Schmidt laid off 20% of staff (the glue people) while keeping salespeople, regulatory staff and product builders, and the CEO received death threats.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Shows which roles survive AI restructuring and the social backlash risk of AI-driven layoffs.

insights.claim: Schmidt says some executives already deploy AI versions of themselves to direct employees and use AI to audit company activity weekly for consistency with values, amplifying decision speed.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Early signal of AI-in-management adoption at small firms.

insights.claim: Schmidt says Europe is losing in AI because regulators regulate before they innovate, universities are underfunded, there is cultural angst about wealth and venture capital is too small, so talent moves to the US.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Supports a structural US-over-Europe tilt in tech equities; European AI upside is policy-dependent.
insights.quote: the regulators regulate before they innovate.

insights.claim: Europe has already lost on energy, chips, cloud and models but can dominate selling AI to Europe itself, because European businesses need regulation-compliant providers; Mistral, where Schmidt was an early investor, does much of its business this way.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: European sovereign/compliant AI vendors have a protected home market.

insights.claim: Schmidt proposed to President Macron that firms with up to 20 employees be exempt from all labor laws except health and safety, to encourage many small bets as Silicon Valley does.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Watch European labor reform as a catalyst for startup formation.

insights.claim: Because Europe has among the world's highest energy costs, Schmidt suggests it train AI models with partner countries such as the Arab states.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Supports Gulf data center build-out as offshore compute for Europe.

insights.claim: ASML shows Europe can build a fully vertically integrated world-critical company, yet Europe has far more software engineers than software companies because firms struggle to scale from local to global platforms.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Europe's bottleneck is scale-up capital formation, not talent.

insights.claim: Europe lacks its own foundation model, so Europeans rely on US- or Chinese-trained models for their own history, language and culture; Schmidt also named Mistral and Helsing as notable European companies.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Sovereign-AI demand in Europe is a policy and investment theme.

insights.claim: Schmidt says a non-growing democracy like Europe begins to fray when new needs such as defense spending arise, while the US keeps growing partly because it prints its own currency.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Low growth plus defense needs points to fiscal strain and political risk in Europe.

insights.claim: Schmidt's team estimates Chinese models are about six months behind US models, as fast followers helped by distillation of Western models and smuggled chips.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: The US lead is thin; export controls are leaky.
insights.quote: It looks like they are six months six months behind.

insights.claim: Even six months behind, the West is already losing on users because Chinese models are free, so most poorer countries will adopt Chinese models over expensive Western ones.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Western labs may win revenue but lose global share; monetization of the Global South will be hard.
insights.quote: if they're six months behind, then we're already losing because their strategy is that the products are free.

insights.claim: China's open-weight strategy lets bad actors strip guardrails from models to enable harms like weapons design, a problem Schmidt says is not yet solved.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Raises odds of regulation targeting open weights; a tail risk for AI policy.

insights.claim: Schmidt says the US banning of Mythos upset Europeans and outside users, that Mythos proved more powerful than he expected, and that a stronger version is coming; China's GLM (Zhipu) may have similar capabilities.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Access restrictions to top US models push non-US users toward alternatives; watch frontier capability jumps.

insights.claim: Schmidt expects AI treaties between the US and China only after an accident, a 'mini Chernobyl' such as a terrorist attack using AI, which would drive regulation.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Regulatory shock risk to AI sector is event-driven; an incident could rapidly change the rules.
insights.quote: So, other people in the industry have said we need a mini Chernobyl.

insights.claim: A recent incident where a swarm of bots attacked a website largely on their own was hard to stop once started, which Schmidt treats as a warning on AI alignment and containment.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Alignment/containment incidents are a growing driver of regulation and security spend.

insights.claim: Schmidt sees AI plus social media as a real threat to democracy because skilled operators can build fake online friends that persuade people of false things as institutional trust declines.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Supports regulation of social platforms and demand for authenticity/identity tools.
insights.quote: You just build fake friends and then you befriend everyone and then everyone believes you.

insights.claim: Public backlash against AI data centers is fuelled by algorithmically amplified false claims, such as that data centers kill cattle, which Schmidt (who builds data centers) found had no evidence.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Local opposition to data centers is a permitting risk for AI infrastructure build-out.

insights.claim: Schmidt calls for urgent regulation of AI and social media with respect to children, this year, citing teen suicides linked to social media.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Child-safety regulation is a near-term policy risk for consumer AI and social platforms.

insights.claim: Founders are returning to lead tech companies because only founders have the control to make big pivots; Mark Zuckerberg spent billions on VR that didn't work well and pivoted to AI, which Schmidt says is working well, while professional CEOs get fired in such transitions.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Favor founder-controlled companies in fast platform transitions.

insights.claim: Schmidt says the key leadership trait now is raw processing and reaction speed, and names his biggest failure as Google not getting ahead in social media while it briefly led.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Leadership speed is a differentiator to weigh when backing tech management teams.

insights.claim: Schmidt is running four new companies to generate wealth for science funding, because the US government is cutting support for basic research, and advises young people to build domain-specific foundation models or agentic systems.
insights.speaker: Eric Schmidt
insights.so_what: Domain foundation models are where Schmidt sees next-generation startup opportunities.
